Nontangential limit (∠limz→0​f(z))

Words: 79 Articles: 1
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
A boundary limit taken while approaching within a cone that stays away from tangency. At zero in the complex upper half-plane, every fixed cone ∣Rez∣≤AImz is allowed. A nontangential limit need not be a limit along all paths approaching the boundary.
// Destination: analysis.bigb

Stolz region (ΓA​(ξ)={z∈D:∣z−ξ∣<A(1−∣z∣)},A>1)

Words: 38
Nontangential limit OurBigBook.com
A fixed-aperture approach region at a boundary point of the unit disc. Its points approach the boundary point without becoming tangent to the circle. Convergence inside every such fixed region is a nontangential limit; the corresponding supremum defines a non-tangential maximal function.

Polynomial hull (K={z:∣p(z)∣≤supK​∣p∣ for every polynomial p})

Words: 135 Articles: 1
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
For a compact set K⊂Cn, its polynomial hull is the set displayed, where p ranges over all complex multivariate polynomials. It contains K. In one complex dimension, bounded complementary components are filled in: the maximum modulus principle bounds every polynomial inside those components by its boundary values. Polynomial approximation and separation distinguish points outside the hull.

Polynomial hull in one complex variable (K)

Words: 81
Polynomial hull OurBigBook.com
For a compact set K⊂C, its polynomial hull is K={z:∣P(z)∣≤supK​∣P∣ for every polynomial P}. In one complex variable this is K together with all bounded components of its complement. The maximum modulus principle proves inclusion of each filled hole. Conversely, polynomial approximation of an exterior pole by the Runge approximation theorem separates an exterior point from the filled compact set. The filled set has connected complement, which makes it the natural set for polynomial approximation of functions whose poles lie in the unbounded complementary component.

Lower half-plane ({z:Imz<0})

Words: 21
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
The lower half-plane is the set of complex numbers with negative imaginary part. It is the reflection of the complex upper half-plane across the real axis.

Holomorphic square root

Words: 78 Articles: 1
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
A holomorphic square root of a nonvanishing holomorphic function f is a holomorphic function g satisfying g2=f. It exists locally, and globally exactly when the winding obstruction around every closed path vanishes.

Entire function OurBigBook.com
An injective holomorphic function cannot have an essential singularity: Casorati-Weierstrass theorem would give values from a small punctured neighbourhood inside the open image of a disjoint neighbourhood, contradicting injectivity. Apply this at infinity to an injective entire function. A removable singularity there would make the function constant by Liouville's theorem. A pole makes it a polynomial by the Cauchy coefficient formula; its derivative has no zero, so the fundamental theorem of algebra forces degree one.

Exponential polynomial (F(z)=∑j​Pj​(z)eλj​z)

Words: 84
Entire function OurBigBook.com
An exponential polynomial is a finite sum of polynomial multiples of exponentials. For distinct exponents, its terms are linearly independent over the polynomial ring: to isolate one term, apply the product of operators (D−λj​)degPj​+1 for all the other terms. On the remaining polynomial each operator becomes D+λ0​−λj​, which is injective because its nonzero constant preserves the leading coefficient. A nonzero exponential polynomial is an entire function of exponential type. Its maximum-modulus logarithm is O(R+logR), and Jensen's formula gives at most O(R) zeros, counted with multiplicity, in a disk of radius R.

This distinction is stronger than mere entire analyticity and controls the genus in Hadamard factorization.

Meromorphic differential on a Riemann surface (ω=f(z)dz)

Words: 90
Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com
A meromorphic differential is specified in each holomorphic chart by a meromorphic coefficient f(z), with the coefficients transforming by the coordinate derivative so that the one-form agrees on overlaps. The derivative of a meromorphic function gives such a differential, and the ratio of two nonzero differentials is a meromorphic function. Orders of zeros and poles are independent of chart because coordinate derivatives are nonvanishing holomorphic factors. On a compact connected surface the sum of orders of a nonzero differential is 2g−2, allowing its divisor to determine the genus.

Hyperbolic Riemann surface in potential theory

Words: 88
Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com
A noncompact Riemann surface is hyperbolic in potential theory when its Green-function exhaustion has a finite limit, equivalently when it admits a positive Green function on a Riemann surface. This definition does not assume a disk uniformization. The unit disk is an example, since −log∣z∣ is its positive Green function with pole zero. For simply connected surfaces this is equivalent to being conformally equivalent to the disk. For general surfaces, potential-theoretic hyperbolicity should not be conflated with the condition that the universal cover is the disk: some surfaces with disk universal cover have no positive Green function.

Compact Riemann surface

Words: 44
Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com
A Riemann surface which is compact as a topological space. For a connected one of genus g, the Riemann-Roch theorem gives g independent holomorphic differential forms. The Riemann bilinear relations for a compact surface make their normalized periods a full lattice in Cg, and the Abel-Jacobi map of a compact Riemann surface turns this lattice into a complex torus encoding divisor classes.

Abel-Jacobi map of a compact Riemann surface (AJ:C(d)→H0(C,KC​)∨/H1​(C,Z))

Words: 133 Articles: 1
Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com
Integration of holomorphic differential forms along cycles embeds the first homology group as a full Euclidean lattice in H0(C,KC​)∨. Fixing a base point, sum the path integrals to the points of an effective complex analytic divisor. Different path choices differ by that lattice. The Abel theorem for divisors identifies the fibres with linear equivalence of divisors.

Abel theorem for divisors

Words: 92
Abel-Jacobi map of a compact Riemann surface OurBigBook.com
A degree-zero complex analytic divisor E on a compact Riemann surface is principal exactly when its Abel-Jacobi map of a compact Riemann surface is zero. Normalize a differential of the third kind with residues equal to the coefficients of E. The Riemann bilinear relations for a compact surface express its b-periods as 2πi times the Abel integrals. If those integrals are in the period lattice, subtract a suitable integral multiple of the normalized holomorphic differential forms; all periods then lie in 2πiZ, so exponentiation gives the required meromorphic function. Conversely, the logarithmic differential of a meromorphic function has integer residues and periods in 2πiZ, giving a zero Abel class by the same calculation.

Words: 74
Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com

Indeed the set of λ∈/K with (u−λ)−1∈A is relatively open by invertibility and relatively closed by uniform continuity of the scalar resolvent; it meets each component by a prescribed pole, or by a Neumann expansion at infinity. It is therefore all of C∖K. Holomorphic functional calculus then places every function holomorphic near K in A, proving prescribed-pole Runge approximation theorem.

The polynomial Runge theorem gives a polynomial within 1/m of a given holomorphic function on Km​. Every compact subset lies in some Km​, so these polynomials converge uniformly on compact subsets.

For each n, take the compact union of the upper rectangle [−n,n]+i[1/n,n], its lower reflection and the real segment [−n,n]. Its complement is connected. The function equal to one, minus one and zero on disjoint neighborhoods of the three components is holomorphic. The polynomial Runge theorem provides a polynomial within 1/n of it on the union. Every fixed point lies in its corresponding component for all large n, proving pointwise convergence. The limit is discontinuous, so the convergence cannot be locally uniform near the real axis. This illustrates how pointwise approximation by holomorphic functions differs from locally uniform approximation.

Entire function confined to a half-plane is constant

Words: 58
Liouville theorem OurBigBook.com
If an entire function g satisfies Re(cg)≥b for constants c=0 and real b, then e−cg is entire and has modulus at most e−b. The Liouville theorem makes it constant, and differentiating gives g′=0 since the exponential never vanishes. The conclusion also applies after rotating and translating any containing half-plane; separate bounds on the real and imaginary parts are unnecessary.

One-sided product bound for an entire function

Words: 55
Liouville theorem OurBigBook.com
If an entire function f=u+iv has uv bounded above, then f is constant. Indeed F=exp(−if2) is entire and ∣F∣=exp(2uv) is bounded, so the Liouville theorem makes F constant. Differentiating gives ff′=0. The derivative of f2 is therefore zero, and continuity on the connected complex plane makes f itself constant. No separate boundedness of u or v is required.

Liouville theorem OurBigBook.com
The image of every nonconstant entire function is dense in C. If a disc about w were omitted, then 1/(f−w) would be bounded and entire, so Liouville's theorem would make f constant.

R−n−1/2∫02π​∣cosθ∣−1/2dθ,

Radial crossing test for polynomial root counts (dtd​log∣z(t)∣=Rezp′(z)1​)

Words: 71
Argument principle OurBigBook.com
If p(z(t))=t and p′(z)=0, implicit differentiation gives z′(t)=1/p′(z). At a crossing of the unit circle, the displayed radial derivative determines whether the root enters or leaves the disk as the real parameter increases. Root counts are constant between such boundary crossings, including multiplicities. At the crossing parameter itself, boundary roots are excluded from an open-disk count. This complements the winding number form of the argument principle and handles a self-intersecting image contour without guessing its enclosed regions.

Quarter-sector winding test for a real quartic

Words: 96
Argument principle OurBigBook.com
Suppose a monic real quartic polynomial has no nonnegative real zero and its real part on the imaginary axis is everywhere positive. For sufficiently large R, its image of the quarter-circle arc from R to iR, closed by the straight chord from p(iR) to p(R), has winding number one: compare with z4 on the arc and its constant image on the chord. The rest of the actual sector boundary maps into the right half-plane, so its replacement by that chord preserves the winding number. The argument principle then counts exactly one root in the open first quadrant, including multiplicity.

Argument principle OurBigBook.com
If f,g are holomorphic near the closure of a bounded domain and ∣g∣<∣f∣ on its boundary, then f and f+g have the same number of interior zeros, counted with multiplicity. Apply the argument principle to the zero-free boundary homotopy f+tg.

Rouché's theorem OurBigBook.com
Let P(z)=∏ℓ​(z−rℓ​) have distinct roots. Choose a disc around rj​ with radius δ smaller than every separation from rj​. On its boundary, ∣P(z)∣≥δ∏ℓ=j​(∣rj​−rℓ​∣−δ). If a holomorphic perturbation H satisfies the displayed inequality, Rouché's theorem shows that P+H has exactly one root in that disc, counted with multiplicity. Discs confined to specified half-planes or quadrants give direct geometric root-location proofs without needing a global root-continuation argument.

The maximum principle for subharmonic functions proves the displayed bound. Zero boundary maxima are handled by adding a positive bound and taking its limit. Words: 39

A maximum-modulus extension for unbounded domains with suitable growth restrictions. In its polynomial-growth vertical-strip form, bounds ∣F(a+it)∣≪(1+∣t∣)u and ∣F(b+it)∣≪(1+∣t∣)v for a holomorphic function imply the interpolated exponent ((b−σ)u+(σ−a)v)/(b−a). It is the strip-convexity tool used to move subpower zeta bounds to the right of the critical line back onto that line.

The real and imaginary parts are harmonic functions, whose mean-value property explains this average identity.

Undetermined coefficient at Frobenius resonance
Words: 83
Frobenius method OurBigBook.com
When two indicial roots differ by a positive integer, the recurrence for the smaller-root Frobenius solution can have a zero coefficient at the index of the larger root. If the corresponding right-hand side also vanishes, that coefficient is free and adds the larger-root solution; if it does not vanish, a pure Frobenius series is obstructed and a logarithmic term may be required. For x2y′′−2xy′−x2y=0, the recurrence n(n−3)an​=an−2​ has a1​=0 and leaves a3​ free. Choosing a3​=0 selects the even solution, not the only solution with exponent zero.

With s=z​ and Y(s)=y(s2), the displayed linear differential equation becomes Yss​+Y=0 away from zero. Its Frobenius solutions have exponents 0 and 1/2: cosz​=∑n≥0​(−1)nzn/(2n)! and sinz​=z1/2∑n≥0​(−1)nzn/(2n+1)!. The first is an entire function of z; the second needs a local square-root branch. This illustrates how a regular singular point can arise from a degenerate change of independent variable.

Frobenius method OurBigBook.com

The equation x2y′′−2xy′+(2−x2)y=0 has a regular singular point at zero. Factoring y=xu cancels the Euler derivative terms and leaves u′′−u=0 away from zero. Its analytic solutions xcoshx and xsinhx extend across zero. Their coefficient recurrence (n−1)(n−2)cn​=cn−2​ has independent free coefficients c1​,c2​, giving two entire solutions without a logarithmic branch despite integer-separated indicial roots.
Terminating Frobenius series
Words: 62
Frobenius method OurBigBook.com
A terminating Frobenius series is a Frobenius method solution whose analytic power series factor has only finitely many nonzero coefficients. Its coefficient linear recurrence relation must allow the first omitted coefficient and all following coefficients to be zero. At an integer separation of characteristic exponents at a regular singular point, a resonant coefficient equation can become 0=0, permitting such a choice rather than forcing a logarithmic term. With exponent zero, termination produces a polynomial solution.

Fuchs relation

Papperitz symbol OurBigBook.com
For a second-order equation with three regular singular points, the sum of all six characteristic exponents is one.
For an order-n Fuchsian differential equation with r finite singular points and infinity, the sum of all characteristic exponents is n(n−1)(r−1)/2. The three-singularity second-order case has n=2 and r=2.

Its local exponents become exactly those of the Gauss hypergeometric equation with parameters (a,b;c): those at one shift by c−a−b, and those at infinity shift by its negative. Direct differentiation gives the same differential equation. Near zero, choose the factor with value one; uniqueness of the analytic normalized solution, for c not a nonpositive integer, gives the identity. Compatible analytic continuation extends it to other domains and parameters where the normalized functions are defined.
